results.summary: This design generates two independent square waves using 8-bit reloadable countdown timers, with periods proportional to the input values plus one. It also provides a 2-bit sum output of the two square waves. The design is tested by applying arbitrary 8-bit values to the inputs and probing the outputs with an oscilloscope or logic analyzer. External hardware is not required, but the intended use is to drive speakers via resistor dividers and an amplifier.

This is a test project created to explore the Chisel hardware construction language. It has 8 inputs, 8 bidirectional pins, and 8 outputs, but the documentation does not describe any specific functionality beyond being a test. The project includes a ChiselTest that can be run with sbt test. No external hardware is required, and the design is notable only as a learning exercise.

This project implements a (7,4) Hamming encoder and decoder with a shared input bus, where the mode is selected by the most significant input bit. In encode mode, it takes a 4-bit input and produces a 7-bit encoded output; in decode mode, it takes a 7-bit input and outputs the corrected 7-bit codeword. Testing involves applying known data and verifying the encoded output, then flipping one bit in the encoded input to confirm error correction. No external hardware is specified, and the design is a straightforward implementation of a classic error-correcting code.

This is a 4x4 structural array multiplier that multiplies two 4-bit unsigned binary numbers to produce an 8-bit product. It uses an array of AND gates and full adders to generate and sum partial products. The design is tested by applying two 4-bit inputs and observing the 8-bit output. No external hardware is needed, and the project appears to be a class assignment for a digital logic course.

This project is a 4x4 array multiplier that takes two 4-bit unsigned numbers and outputs their 8-bit product. It is built from 12 full adders and 16 AND gates, following a structural array multiplier architecture. Testing is done by applying two 4-bit inputs via the ui_in pins and reading the product on the uo_out pins. No external hardware is required, and the design is a typical class project for learning digital arithmetic.

This is a 4x4 structural array multiplier that multiplies two 4-bit binary numbers to produce an 8-bit result. It generates 16 partial products using AND gates and sums them with full adders. The design is tested by applying various 4-bit inputs in a simulation environment and verifying the product. No external hardware is needed, and the project is a standard educational implementation of an array multiplier.

This project implements a 4-bit array multiplier that computes the product of two 4-bit unsigned numbers, outputting an 8-bit result. It uses partial product generation with AND gates and summation with full adders. Testing is done by applying an 8-bit input representing two 4-bit numbers and checking the 8-bit output. No external hardware is required, and the design is a straightforward educational example of a structural multiplier.

This is a 4x4 array multiplier that multiplies two 4-bit unsigned binary numbers to produce an 8-bit product. It is implemented structurally using logic gates and 1-bit full adders, following a partial product and addition approach. The design can be tested via an automatic testbench or by building the circuit from provided schematics. No external hardware is used, and the project is a class assignment for a digital logic course.

This design displays the letters of 'SEnOLGULGONUL' on a 7-segment display using an internal three-gate ring oscillator. It requires external resistors and a capacitor to complete the oscillator circuit, and the outputs connect directly to a 7-segment display. Testing involves connecting the external components and observing the letters on the display. The project is notable for using a simple gate-based oscillator to drive a text display.

This project implements a shifter that outputs the result of shifting the 8-bit input right by the number of positions specified on the 8-bit bidirectional input. The design is tested by setting switches on the inputs and observing the shifted value on LEDs connected to the outputs. No external hardware beyond switches and LEDs is required. The documentation is minimal, describing only the basic operation.
